deep.reconstruction:
NOTATION (fixed by the opening assumption). Write Π(y,x) = ∏_{k≥0}(1 + y x^k) = (−y;x)_∞, with |x|<1. The assumed formula Π(b,x)/Π(−a,x) = 1 + (a+b)/(1−x) + (a+b)(a+bx)/((1−x)(1−x^2)) + ... is the q-binomial theorem. Its n-th term is a^n(−b/a;x)_n/(x;x)_n, and the sum is (−b;x)_∞/(a;x)_∞. Throughout, [n,k] denotes the Gaussian binomial (x;x)_n/((x;x)_k(x;x)_{n−k}).

(1) Finite q-binomial theorem (Rothe/Cauchy). For a positive integer n:
∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(c − x^j) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k x^{k(k−1)/2} [n,k] c^{n−k}.
The printed terms are k = 0,1,2,3: c^n − c^{n−1}(1−x^n)/(1−x) + c^{n−2}·x·[n,2] − c^{n−3}·x^3·[n,3] + ...
This is the elementary-symmetric-function expansion, since e_k(1,x,…,x^{n−1}) = x^{k(k−1)/2}[n,k]. Ramanujan says it 'can be proved' from the assumed series; one natural route (mine) is to compare coefficients in the q-binomial theorem with b = −a x^n.

(2) Inverse relation (a q-analogue of c^n = Σ C(n,k)(c−1)^k):
c^n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} [n,k] ∏_{j=0}^{k−1}(c − x^j).
His justification: the coefficient of c^n on the right is 1 (from k = n). For r<n, the coefficient of c^r, after expanding each product by (1), is an alternating Gaussian-binomial sum that vanishes; Ramanujan only says it vanishes 'by applying (1)'. A check is easy: n = 2 gives 1 + (c−1)(1+x) + (c−1)(c−x) = c^2.

(3) Main computation. He compares coefficients of a^n in
S = Σ_{k≥0} a^k ∏_{j<k}(x^j − b)(x^j − c)/(x;x)_k · Π(−a x^k, x)/Π(−ab, x).
The printed terms are k = 0,1,2: (1−b)(1−c)/(1−x) and (1−b)(x−b)(1−c)(x−c)/((1−x)(1−x^2)).

Step A. Apply the assumed formula with a→ab, b→−ax^k:
Π(−ax^k,x)/Π(−ab,x) = Σ_m a^m ∏_{j=k}^{k+m−1}(b − x^j)/(x;x)_m.
So the k-th term contributes to a^n the amount
∏_{j<k}(x^j−b)(x^j−c)/(x;x)_k · ∏_{j=k}^{n−1}(b−x^j)/(x;x)_{n−k}.
The k = 0, 1, 2 cases are exactly the three displayed terms. For k = 2 the second numerator should be (b−x^2)…(b−x^{n−1}); see errors.

Step B. Note (1−b)(1−c) = (b−1)(c−1), and generally ∏_{j<k}(x^j−b)(x^j−c) = ∏_{j<k}(b−x^j)(c−x^j). Pulling out the common factor gives
coefficient = ∏_{j<n}(b−x^j)/(x;x)_n · Σ_k [n,k] ∏_{j<k}(c−x^j).
This is his last displayed line, the brace {1 + (c−1)(1−x^n)/(1−x) + (c−1)(c−x)[n,2] + …}.

Completion (my addition; the page stops here). By (2) the brace equals c^n. So the coefficient is c^n ∏_{j<n}(b−x^j)/(x;x)_n. By the assumed formula, that is the coefficient of a^n in Π(−ac,x)/Π(−abc,x) = (ac;x)_∞/(abc;x)_∞. Hence
Σ_k a^k ∏_{j<k}(x^j−b)(x^j−c)/(x;x)_k · (ax^k;x)_∞/(ab;x)_∞ = (ac;x)_∞/(abc;x)_∞.

Rewriting. Multiply by (ab;x)_∞/(a;x)_∞ and set B = 1/b, C = 1/c:
Σ_k (B;x)_k(C;x)_k/((x;x)_k(a;x)_k) · (a/(BC))^k = (a/B;x)_∞(a/C;x)_∞/((a;x)_∞(a/(BC);x)_∞).
This is the q-Gauss (Heine) summation of 2φ1(B,C;a;x,a/BC).

Purpose. The page is a lemma in a chain toward a summation needed for the Rogers–Ramanujan functions; the pencil annotation reads 'Rogers-R fu[nctio]n[s]'. The next page continues 'Proof of final formula completed if…'.
errors: Third displayed term of (3): the coefficient of a^{n−2} in Π(−ax^2,x)/Π(−ab,x) is (b−x^2)(b−x^3)…(b−x^{n−1})/((1−x)…(1−x^{n−2})). The manuscript's numerator begins with (b−x), i.e. it repeats the factor already supplied by (x−b) in the prefactor. The upper end has been amended in fainter ink to include (b−x^{n−1}), and the denominator end has been altered to (1−x^{n−2}). Ramanujan was evidently correcting the indices, but the starting factor (b−x) remains a slip (it should be (b−x^2)).
Step (2) is only sketched: the vanishing of the coefficients of c^r for r<n via (1) is asserted, not carried out. It is true.
Implicit conditions |x|<1 and |a|,|ab|,|abc|<1, needed for convergence of the infinite products and series, are not stated.
The page stops before invoking (2) to replace the brace by c^n and before stating the resulting identity; the conclusion (q-Gauss sum) is a reconstruction.

results.modern_name: q-analogue of c^n = Σ C(n,k)(c−1)^k; Gaussian inverse relation / q-Newton interpolation (combinatorially Goldman–Rota counting linear maps)
results.usually_credited_to: classical (19th c.; Cauchy/Gauss-type identities), combinatorial form Goldman–Rota 1970

results.what: (3) Coefficient comparison giving Σ_k a^k ∏_{j<k}(x^j−b)(x^j−c)/(x;x)_k · (ax^k)_∞/(ab)_∞ = (ac)_∞/(abc)_∞, equivalently 2φ1(B,C;a;x,a/BC) = (a/B)_∞(a/C)_∞/((a)_∞(a/BC)_∞)
results.modern_name: q-Gauss summation (Heine's q-analogue of Gauss's 2F1(1) sum), proved by coefficient comparison

deep.surprise_reason: Everything on the page is classical q-series: the q-binomial theorem, its finite form, the Gaussian inverse relation, and the q-Gauss/Heine summation. Ramanujan's notebooks are known to contain these, and his use of them in Rogers–Ramanujan work is documented. The coefficient-comparison proof via the c^n expansion is a pleasant elementary route but not historically significant.

transcription_corrections: Third term of (3): the factor '(b−x^{n−1})' is a later fainter insertion appended after (b−x^{n−2}), and the denominator's final factor is overwritten as (1−x^{n−2}). The bracketed '{+ … +}' and '[− … −]' in the machine transcription are artifacts of this.
In (2) the left side is lowercase c^n (the transcription's 'C^n' is the same symbol).
Pencil annotation reads approximately 'Rogers-R fu[nctio]ns' (Rogers–Ramanujan functions), circled — an archivist's or editor's note, not Ramanujan's hand.
